schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make Saul's ruin the introduction to the history of David's kingship; Ellicott carries the battle itself, the plain of Jezreel, the collective singular for the fleeing men, and the rendering 'he shuddered before the shooters'.
Henry reads the fall as judgement in kind: the javelin thrown at David answered by the archers, Doeg's commission by the armour-bearer's, the spared Amalekites by a servant's disobedience.
Clarke, finding the account almost word for word the same as the older one, declines to comment and refers the reader back to his notes on 1 Samuel 31.

debates.issue: Whether the archers wounded Saul or only terrified him

positions.view: Henry's correspondence of sins to punishments requires that the archers hit the king who had thrown a javelin at David and missed.
Ellicott renders the verb as to writhe or travail and has Saul shudder before the shooters, the terror being natural in a man who believed himself forsaken of God.

1.pericope_label: The Philistines fought against Israel: Saul fell upon his sword

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the local conception of deity implied in sending the head round, traces Ashtaroth from Ascalon to Nineveh, and argues the skull in the house of Dagon against the corpse on the wall of Beth-shan points to a second source rather than corruption.

Henry draws three lessons: dignity exposes a man to disgrace, a victory whose glory is not given to God is condemned by the Philistines' own practice, and the remains of the dead are owed respect without enquiry into the eternal state.

Clarke refers the motive of the men of Jabesh to heroism and gratitude and promises a fuller illustration at the chapter's end; Wesley carries over Henry's question about Dagon's share in the triumph.

debates.issue: Whether the divergences from the older account are corruption or a second source

positions.view: Ellicott calls it hardly likely that either the skull in Dagon's house or the corpse on the wall of Beth-shan is a corruption of the other, and takes the terebinth against the tamarisk as a further mark of an additional source.

themes: the idols that must be told of the victory
burial and the seven days' fast
8.pericope_label: They stripped him and took his head: the valiant men of Jabesh arose

schools.summary: Ellicott sets the unfaithfulness out as twofold, the prophetic word unobserved and a necromancer consulted, notices that the verdict passes over the slaughter of the priests, and answers the clause that God slew him by the instrumentality of His creatures.

Clarke gives the Targum, which supplies the priests of Nob as a third count, and appends a correspondent's letter on the gratitude of Jabesh and the Homeric honour paid to the bodies of fallen chiefs; Wesley grades the failed enquiry by its manner and its lateness.
Gill allows that Saul enquired in an external, careless and hypocritical manner, so that it was accounted as no enquiry, and refuses the Targum's added count as not in the text.

debates.issue: Whether the slaughter of the priests belongs among the reasons for Saul's death

positions.view: Ellicott observes only that no allusion is made to it, nor to Saul's hatred of David.
Clarke reproduces the Targum, which makes the slain priests of Nob the reason no answer came by Urim and Thummim.
Gill reports the same addition and rejects it on the ground that it is not in the text.

outliers.view: A letter from a literary friend argues the men of Jabesh acted from gratitude for their rescue from Nahash, and sets the contest for Saul's body beside the Homeric struggles over a fallen chief and the hero of the Iliad's treatment of Hector.

themes: the priests of Nob and the Targum
13.pericope_label: So Saul died for his transgression: he enquired not of the Lord
